items.title: Vacature directeur / bestuurder
items.raw_text: Wil jij richting geven aan een organisatie die overheid, bedrijfsleven, kenniswereld en maatschappij bij elkaar brengt op het gebied van digitalisering? Kun jij maatschappelijke en bestuurlijke vraagstukken verbinden aan concrete samenwerking én zorgen voor een professionele en toekomstbestendige organisatie? Dan is dit jouw kans om betekenisvolle impact te maken. Binnen Stichting ECP | Platform voor de InformatieSamenleving is namelijk de vacature ontstaan voor een: directeur-bestuurder Wat ga je doen? ECP heeft al ruim 25 jaar een bewezen meerwaarde door haar verbindende kracht, neutrale opstelling en breed gedragen en geïmplementeerde resultaten van programma’s en projecten. ECP bevindt zich op dit moment in een belangrijke fase in haar ontwikkeling: in de periode 2026–2028 werkt ECP aan een transitie gericht op het borgen van continuïteit, het professionaliseren van de governance en het toekomstbestendig maken van de organisatie, met behoud van de kernwaarden. De Directeur-Bestuurder fungeert als boegbeeld en stuurt op deze transitie. Daarbij geldt dat je niet primair technisch verantwoordelijk bent voor dagelijkse procesuitvoering, maar wel borgt dat ECP intern voldoende in samenhang is georganiseerd, zodat governance, kwaliteit en financiële beheersing op orde zijn. Je geeft leiding aan ECP als platform en vormt daarbij de spil tussen extern betekenis geven, bestuurlijke besluitvaardigheid en interne bestuurbaarheid. items.title: Nederlanders denken dat ze phishing herkennen, maar AI maakt oplichting steeds echter en juist dát is een groot veiligheidsrisico
items.raw_text: Uit het jaarlijkse nationale cybersecurityonderzoek van Alert Online, mede mogelijk gemaakt door het ministerie van Economische Zaken en Klimaat, blijkt dat Nederlanders wél weten wat veilig online gedrag is, maar gemiddeld slechts een derde van de veilige handelingen consequent toepassen. Den Haag – Nederlanders weten goed hoe ze zich online moeten beschermen, maar vertrouwen opvallend vaak op hun eigen vermogen om gevaar te herkennen. Zodra er meer van hen gevraagd wordt dan kijken, neemt de motivatie om zich veilig te gedragen af. Slechts één op de zes gebruikt altijd tweefactorauthenticatie, een dubbel slot voor je accounts en apparaten dat ervoor zorgt dat er meer nodig is dan een wachtwoord om in te loggen. Zo kunnen criminelen met een gestolen wachtwoord niet zomaar een account overnemen. En maar drie op de tien gaan altijd zelf naar de officiële website in plaats van op een link te klikken. Dat blijkt uit het nationale cybersecurityonderzoek van Alert Online, dat vandaag verschijnt bij de start van de Europese cybersecuritymaand. Wie denkt zelf phishing te herkennen, slaat in veel gevallen de stappen over die je écht beschermen. Ook weten mensen vaak niet hóé ze iets instellen, zien ze anderen het niet doen en voelt het als te veel werk. items.title: Podcastaflevering over Digitaal Doordacht en de praktijkimpact van digitalisering
items.raw_text: ECP-directeur Arie van Bellen ging in een recente aflevering van de podcastreeks ECP Talks in gesprek met ECP-programmaregisseur Sabine Herbrink over het programma Digitaal Doordacht. Zij bespraken hoe het programma de overheid helpt om bewuste, doordachte keuzes te maken in onze snel digitaliserende samenleving. Het gesprek ging niet alleen over de kansen zoals dwarsverbanden tussen thema’s en de meerwaarde die het programma biedt in de digitalisering van de overheid, maar ook over de uitdagingen rondom verantwoorde inzet, innovatie en samenwerking. Meer weten? Beluister de aflevering ‘Praktijkimpact van digitalisering’ Het bericht Podcastaflevering over Digitaal Doordacht en de praktijkimpact van digitalisering verscheen eerst op ECP | Platform voor de InformatieSamenleving .

items.title: Van regisserende naar ontwerpende overheid
items.raw_text: Van AI-experiment naar digitaal opdrachtgeverschap Veranderverhalen vanuit ECP | Platform voor de Informatiesamenleving ECP | Platform voor de Informatiesamenleving brengt met een reeks veranderverhalen in beeld hoe professionals binnen de overheid werken aan betekenisvolle digitalisering. In de gesprekken met Marc Minnee en Marco de Bruijn van het ministerie van Binnenlandse Zaken en Koninkrijksrelaties (BZK) staat centraal waar verandering daadwerkelijk ontstaat: wanneer professionals elkaar vinden, aannames bespreekbaar maken en keuzes maken die bijdragen aan versnelling én duurzame borging. Zo laten de verhalen zien hoe digitalisering door concrete interventies kan bijdragen aan een toekomstgerichte overheid waarin burgers en ondernemers centraal staan, met blijvende aandacht voor ethiek, privacy, security en maatschappelijk vertrouwen. Op 24 juni vond in Amare voor de vijfde keer de CIO-dag plaats. Voor een zaal vol CIO’s schetsten Marc Minnee, innovatiemanager voor het ministerie van BZK, en Marco de Bruijn, beleidsmedewerker AI bij het ministerie van BZK, hun NDS AI-visie op de inzet van generatieve AI-modellen bij de overheid. Hun verhaal begint bij taalmodellen, maar raakt al snel aan een veel fundamentelere vraag: hoe houdt de overheid zelf regie over haar digitale toekomst? Binnen de Nederlandse Digitaliseringsstrategie is AI daarom een prioriteit: de overheid wil AI verantwoord inzetten voor maatschappelijke opgaven en betere dienstverlening, succesvolle toepassin

items.title: OTC Whitepaper Soevereiniteit
items.raw_text: Digitale soevereiniteit betekent niet dat organisaties alle digitale diensten zelf moeten bezitten of beheren. Het betekent dat zij aantoonbare grip hebben op kritieke digitale afhankelijkheden: inzicht in de keten, bewuste risicoacceptatie, uitvoerbare alternatieven, onafhankelijke controle en transparante communicatie over keuzes en restrisico’s. In het whitepaper over digitale soevereiniteit vertaalt de Online Trust Coalitie dit thema naar een praktisch handelingskader voor bestuurders, IT-verantwoordelijken, toezichthouders, serviceproviders en risk- en compliancefuncties. De OTC stelt dat digitale soevereiniteit niet draait om volledige autonomie of autarkie, maar om aantoonbare beheersing: inzicht in kritieke digitale afhankelijkheden, expliciete risicoafweging, uitvoerbare exit-mogelijkheden, onafhankelijke controle en heldere communicatie over restrisico’s en gemaakte keuzes. De OTC signaleert dat impliciet vertrouwen in digitale diensten onder druk staat. Geopolitieke spanningen, conflicterende rechtsstelsels, concentratie van leveranciersmacht en complexe beheerketens maken zichtbaar dat organisaties niet langer kunnen volstaan met contracten, certificaten of algemene toezeggingen. items.title: ‘Veranderen doe je via consensus én met fermheid’
items.raw_text: Binnen Digitaal Doordacht onderzoeken we hoe digitalisering in de publieke sector daadwerkelijk bijdraagt aan betere dienstverlening, meer openheid en groter vertrouwen. Het veranderverhaal van Jolein Baidenmann laat zien dat echte openheid niet draait om simpelweg méér informatie openbaar maken, maar om informatie die voor mensen daadwerkelijk begrijpelijk en bruikbaar is. Wat haar aanpak bijzonder maakt, is hoe zij in een complexe publieke omgeving beweging creëert: door belangen zichtbaar te maken, partijen te verbinden en draagvlak te combineren met duidelijke keuzes. “Soms moet je als leider keuzes maken en stevig zijn: ik heb iedereen gehoord, maar we gaan toch die kant op.” Jolein Baidenmann is verandermanager en werkt met die insteek aan een overheid die openheid op een betekenisvolle manier probeert waar te maken. “Het is belangrijk dat een open overheid de samenleving in staat stelt om mee te denken, te controleren en gebruik te maken van de informatie die bij de overheid beschikbaar is.” Als manager Open Overheid en plaatsvervangend directeur Open Overheid bij het ministerie van Binnenlandse Zaken en Koninkrijksrelaties (BZK) is Baidenmann bij uitstek de persoon om het concept ‘open overheid’ in praktijk te brengen. Sommigen bepleiten ‘radicale openbaarheid’, wat simpelweg neerkomt op álles openbaar maken. items.title: Metropolitan Libraries Spotlight: How Nanhai Library Is Reconnecting Children with the Classics
items.raw_text: When a thousand-year-old novel has to compete with a 15-second video In Foshan, in the heart of the Guangdong-Hong Kong-Macao Greater Bay Area, Nanhai Library serves a district of more than 3.7 million people, where local families, migrant workers, students, and seniors intertwine in a fast-moving, diverse community. It is also a community facing a very contemporary problem: as short-form video quietly absorbs every spare moment of screen time, deep reading is being pushed to the margins, even when the content at stake is centuries old. Rather than treat this as a lost cause, the library decided to meet children where their attention already lives. In April 2026, it launched Classics 101: Mental Models for Kids, a program built specifically for 10- to 12-year-olds — the exact age when children move from picture-to-text bridge books into more demanding reading. Making the classics legible again The challenge was concrete and specific. More than 60% of students in the first sessions admitted their biggest frustration was simple: they could not remember who everyone was or how all the characters connected. The semi-archaic language, sprawling character webs, and unhurried pacing of China’s Four Great Classical Novels were never designed to compete with instant gratification. So Nanhai Library stopped asking children to memorize plots and started extracting something more useful: practical mental models drawn directly from the characters’ journeys. items.title: Learning by Doing: IFLA Futures Club #5
items.raw_text: The fifth edition of the IFLA Futures Club offered an opportunity to explore what it looks like to apply futures thinking in libraries, in reality. Erik Boekesteijn and Cathelijne Kuiters of the Dutch National Library (KB) joined us to talk about their experience of running a concerted initiative to make futures thinking a more central part of the institution’s work, both with a view to shaping a new policy plan, and building skills more broadly. This was not the first time that futures had been on the agenda at the KB. Already, a ‘Club Stof’ had brought together colleagues throughout the sector, keen to get to grips with ‘the uncomfortable uncertainty of the future’. But with awareness that we are in a time where pre-existing ideas and assumptions are being challenged – epistemic turbulence – the Library’s new leadership was ready to take this work up a gear. There was an awareness from the start that this work provided an opportunity to think more broadly. First of all, an initaitive like this in the KB is not just an internal exercise, but also has potential impacts across the wider library field. National libraries usually have a kind of leadership within their fields, but the Dutch one has a formal role in supporting the country’s network of national libraries. What it does has the possibility to feed into changes across every local authority in the country. items.title: Open science opens the process, not just the paper
items.raw_text: Beyond open access There is no doubt that open access has made major progress: about half of all papers are now published open access worldwide. However, making a paper readable is only the first step and “readable in the sense of open access doesn’t mean reliable or ready for replication,” remarked Prof. Robin Wilkening in the October 6th, 2026 webinar Beyond Open Access: Open Science Across the Entire Research Cycle , co-hosted by the Science and Technology Libraries Section and the Advisory Committee on Open Science and Scholarship . A scientific paper is only the tip of the iceberg. Beneath it are the research question, hypothesis, methods, protocols, instruments, data, code, and reviews that make the research possible. If these remain inaccessible, researchers are simply unable to replicate published findings. Wilkening, therefore, argues for open science across the entire research cycle, rather than focusing only on the final publication. Opening the research cycle Openness can begin with funding and continue through study design, data collection, analysis, publication, evaluation, and reuse. Researchers can pre-register their hypotheses and analysis plans, make instruments and tools open, deposit data and code in repositories, and use preprints to make findings available for discussion before the journal publication process is complete. items.title: IFLA at 100: Looking Back on the ARL Blog
items.raw_text: Mimi Calter, Chair The IFLA Academic & Research Libraries Section is very happy to have you as a reader of our blog! The section has had a blog since 2012, typically posting twice a month, and in that time we’ve been able to publish some remarkable pieces. We are very proud of the history represented in those years of publishing. Unfortunately, much of that history is no longer easily linkable. In 2025, for administrative reasons, we had to retire the WordPress platform that we had been using and transition to the IFLA website as our host site. All of our old posts are preserved, in multiple formats, and are publicly accessible through the IFLA repository (URI: https://repository.ifla.org/handle/20.500.14598/7439 ). However, we no longer have a way to link readers directly to those older posts. To address this issue, and in the spirit of celebrating 100 years of IFLA, we will be introducing a “Looking Back” feature to our blog. We will republish some of our most noteworthy blog posts from the past, sometimes with an update if there is new news to share. The Looking Back posts will be an addition to our ongoing blog postings. If you have a favorite post from the past, let us know! We’ll be happy to add that content to the Looking Back series. And we hope you enjoy looking back and forward!

items.title: The Europe Regional Division Proudly Presents Itself! Webinar recording now available
items.raw_text: On 1 October 2026 , the IFLA Europe Regional Division welcomed library professionals, information specialists and IFLA members from across Europe to the webinar The Europe Regional Division Proudly Presents Itself! The event provided an opportunity to learn more about the work of the Europe Regional Division Committee (EURDC) and the ways in which it supports the library community across Europe. Committee members Antti Sauli (Finland), Arne Gundersen (Norway), Juliana Pranke (Germany) and Zélia Parreira (Portugal) presented current activities and priorities, while also inviting participants to share their expectations and ideas for the future. The discussion offered useful feedback on the needs and interests of European library professionals. Among the topics mentioned most frequently were copyright issues and library statistics. Participants also expressed interest in further online events covering a variety of subjects relevant to libraries and information services. The webinar highlighted the importance of maintaining an open dialogue with the European library community. The comments and suggestions received will help the Committee plan future activities and ensure that the Division continues to respond to the interests of its members. The recording is now available on our new YouTube channel ! If you were unable to join the live session, we invite you to watch the recording and share it with colleagues who may be interested. items.title: Out Now: Ocotober 2026 issue of IFLA Journal
items.raw_text: IFLA Journal is an international journal publishing peer reviewed articles on library and information services and the social, political and economic issues that impact access to information through libraries. The Journal publishes research, case studies and essays that reflect the broad spectrum of the profession internationally. IFLA Journal Volume 52, No.3 (October 2026) The October 2026 edition of IFLA Journal includes 19 articles focused on libraries’ responses to technological change, social challenges, and evolving community needs. Contributions include an essay that documents the impact of war on Ukrainian public librarians plus original research on artificial intelligence applications and equitable access through disability inclusion. items.title: Australian Public Libraries Statistical Report 2024–25
items.raw_text: Australians are using their public libraries in growing numbers, with visits, borrowing and participation in library programs continuing to rise despite increasing pressure on funding and staffing. The Australian Public Libraries Statistical Report 2024–25 , released by the Australian Library and Information Association (ALIA) and National and State Libraries Australasia (NSLA), provides a national snapshot of public library services and how Australians are using them. The figures tell a good news story, with Australian communities increasingly turning to their public libraries for collections, spaces, online services, programs and activities. Physical and online library visits increased by 8.5% in a single year, reaching a five-year high of more than 160 million visits. Public library collections were used almost 180 million times, while a record 434,000 library programs attracted more than 7.2 million attendees. Digital engagement also continues to grow, with digital collection use increasing by 80% over five years and Wi-Fi use almost doubling since 2021–22. Libraries are increasingly being used as places to meet, work and connect, with meeting-room use up 24% in the past year and 81% since 2021–22. Despite the steady increase in usage, public libraries are meeting this heightened demand within an increasingly constrained funding environment. In 2025, 4,235 titles were banned or challenged at public, school, or university libraries, according to the American Library Association’s (ALA) State of America’s Libraries 2026 report. This figure was the second highest (following the record set in 2023) since ALA’s Office for Intellectual Freedom (OIF) began documenting censorship attempts in 1990. items.title: Refreshing for the Future
items.raw_text: Library renovations can feel overwhelming—especially when you’re juggling tight budgets, big community expectations, and a building that’s showing its age. The good news is you don’t have to choose between “do nothing” and “tear it down.” Most successful library upgrades live somewhere in the middle: a smart, phased plan that protects your long-term vision while making meaningful improvements right now. Here are a few practical ways to think about approaching a library renovation: Start with a North Star. Before you pick finishes or start talking timelines, take a step back and get clarity on what you want your library to become. I call this the north star —your vision for how the building should function for staff and the public. Even if you only have funding for part of the work today, guiding principles help you avoid spending money on changes you’ll undo later. Renovations are much easier when everyone can point to the same end goal—even if you’re getting there in phases. Assess the building first. It’s tempting to jump straight into visible improvements, but understanding existing conditions is what sets a project up for success. A solid facility-condition evaluation looks at the status of major building systems and flags components that may be nearing the end of their life cycle, such as mechanical systems, electrical panel capacity, and even finishes like carpet. items.title: Limiting Risk in the Face of Uncertainty
items.raw_text: If you save for retirement when you are young, the standard advice is to emphasize stock-based exchange-traded funds (ETFs) or mutual funds. Stocks increase and decrease in dramatic ways that no one can predict reliably, so this approach carries some risk. Fortunately for US stock market investors, that risk has historically been rewarded, on average and over the long term, with high returns. As you approach retirement and need to rely on investments to cover living expenses, the standard advice is to shift your portfolio toward bond-based ETFs or mutual funds. Bonds have had fewer and less dramatic booms and busts. For this reason, they are generally considered less risky than stocks. On average, over the long term, bonds’ safety has meant lower, more reliable returns than stocks. Risk makes less sense for ALA right now. Because of its financial deficit , the Association needs stability. Therefore, in April, ALA’s Endowment Trustees updated the target allocation for the Association’s investment portfolio, reducing our holdings of stocks from 50% to 40%, and increasing ALA’s holdings of bonds from 30% to 40%. As a result, we are sacrificing some projected returns to limit projected risk. If stocks boom as they have in the past few years, ALA’s portfolio will not increase as much as it would have. items.title: Secrets of Effective Upskilling
items.raw_text: This is an excerpt from Upskilling for Library Workers: A Guide for Future-Ready Professionals by Ann Medaille (ALA Editions, 2026). With the advent of new technologies and rapid social and economic shifts, library workers’ jobs are being transformed. Compared with a decade ago, library workers now spend more time consulting on complex research tools, teaching digital literacy classes, supporting virtual learning environments, helping users troubleshoot devices, and codesigning projects with community partners. The pace at which library staffers are called upon to learn new skills is accelerating, and workers may struggle to keep up. In addition, automation and artificial intelligence (AI) are altering many aspects of work. In the long run, technological innovations have the potential to increase productivity and lead to more interesting kinds of work, but in the short term, they often cause disruptions that can be difficult for workers to navigate. To address these changes—and manage the anxieties that come along with them—workers need constant support for skill development. While corporations may embrace upskilling to stay competitive, libraries will have to support upskilling to remain relevant. Library leaders are under greater pressure to respond rapidly to changing social and economic conditions and demonstrate that their libraries make a difference in their communities. items.title: Hold the Phone
items.raw_text: Since fall 2024, each school day at Grant High School in Portland, Oregon, has started the same way: Roughly 2,100 students line up to place their phones in gray and green Yondr pouches—the kind live performers use to prevent audience members from recording—as they enter the building. From the morning bell to dismissal, phones are sealed and can be unlocked only with special magnets near the school’s exits as students leave for the day. The high school’s effort to limit phone use on campus has received support from its educators, who say classroom engagement is on the rise, and mixed reviews from students, who dislike being cut off from their devices. But there’s been one unexpected outcome of the policy: More students are spending time in the library, where they’re browsing the collection or hanging out during free periods, says teacher-librarian Paige Battle. “They’re checking out more books, and I feel like that’s been so important in their education,” Battle says. “We’re seeing studies about students, even adults, not having the reading stamina they’ve had in the past, so I’ve been encouraged by this increase.” Roughly six in 10 parents of an 11- or 12-year-old say their child owns a smartphone, according to a 2025 Pew Research Center survey . And as more schools across the country enact phone-free policies—29 states and the District of Columbia have instituted bell-to-bell phone-free policies so far—many school libraries are experiencing a surge in popularity. items.raw_text: Buffeted by Change, Researchers Seek Continuity and Investment: Results from the Ithaka S+R US Researcher Survey was written by: Chelsea McCracken Dylan Ruediger Ruby MacDougall From the Report’s Executive Summary: The research enterprise in the United States, established after the second world war, is experiencing massive disruption. US colleges and universities are grappling with federal and state disinvestment and intervention at a time when AI and other technologies are reshaping how research is conducted and its findings are communicated. As a result, researchers at US higher education institutions are operating in an unstable environment. Against this backdrop, the findings from our survey of 4,003 researchers, fielded in late 2025, demonstrate that they remain committed to carrying out essential work and that they are doing so in innovative ways—through collaboration, the creation of valuable educational experiences, and pushing knowledge towards the next frontier. While researchers don’t necessarily agree on how their sector should respond to the changing environment, our findings underscore the importance of stability, continuity, and sustained investment. items.title: Elena, Aris, Marcus: : AI-Generated ‘Ghosts’ are Polluting the Scientific Literature
items.raw_text: From Nature: Elena Vasquez spent three months camping on the rim of Mount Nyiragongo in the Democratic Republic of the Congo back in 2019. She says the sulfur dioxide there smelt like “burnt matches mixed with rotten eggs”. Her colleague, Marcus Chen, has witnessed 11 volcanic eruptions across four continents. Vasquez and Chen’s accounts appeared on Volcanoes Explored, a now-defunct website that described itself as a resource for “exploring the dynamic world of volcanoes”. But there’s a problem: these tales are not real and the pair of volcanology specialists is made up. Vasquez and Chen are ‘ghost’ identities generated by Claude — the large language model (LLM) made by Anthropic in San Francisco — when prompted by users to create fictional experts, according to a preprint published in June. Gemini, Google’s LLM, was found to use a different pair of recurring characters, called Aris Thorne and Lena Petrova, and OpenAI’s GPT repeatedly used the name Elara Voss. [Clip] Fake experts such as these can be found across the Internet as everything from blockchain specialists and astronauts to board members and podcast hosts, and they raise specific concerns around integrity of the scientific literature, say Neo Christopher Chung and Michał Brzozowski, computer scientists at the Samsung AI Center Warsaw in Poland and co-authors of the preprint. items.title: Mellon Foundation Releases: “Mapping the Landscape of Community-Based Archives” Report
items.raw_text: From the Mellon Foundation: Today, the Mellon Foundation released “Powerful but Precarious: Mapping the Landscape of Community-Based Archives,” the first national study of its kind. Produced in partnership with research firm Engage R+D, the study draws on a survey of 336 independent, community-led archives, and in-depth interviews with more than 20 practitioners across the country. Community-based archives are independent organizations that collect and preserve the records, photographs, oral histories, personal papers, and other artifacts of communities many of which have been historically excluded from mainstream institutions. Unlike institutional archives, community-based archives often hold materials that exist nowhere else – collections that, if lost, cannot be recovered. Additionally, community-based archives often operate outside of the context of universities, libraries, historical societies, or other collecting institutions and in doing so, they serve as civic infrastructure where people can access and learn about their own localized or underexplored histories. While hundreds of these archives exist across the United States, serving communities of every background and geography, they have never been mapped, counted, or examined at this scale—leaving them largely invisible to the funders, policymakers, and organizations best positioned to support them. items.title: Report: Chinese-Owned Science Journal Created to Rival the Best
items.raw_text: From Nature: A new Chinese-owned journal has set its sights on rivalling the world’s oldest and most influential academic titles. Vita is one of several English-language journals that have launched in China in the past couple of years. They represent the country’s latest effort to create prestigious global journals, as part of the government’s Journal Excellence Action Plan, which began in 2019. [Clip] Vita is jointly funded by the Higher Education Press, a subsidiary of China’s Ministry of Education based in Beijing, and Westlake University in Hangzhou, its editorial team says. It publishes papers in biological sciences. Its first print issue came out in July. As an open-access journal, Vita waives article-processing charges (APCs), fees many publishers require authors to pay when publishing open access articles. [Clip] Vita ’s model is “clearly going to be appealing” to authors, says James Butcher, a former publisher who runs a consultancy firm called Journalology near Liverpool, UK. But he warns that keeping the model running in the long term will be a challenge for the journal and its funders because “publishing is expensive”. Publishers who charge APCs say that the money helps to cover the costs of publishing open access, including paying the salaries of in-house editors and production staff, as well as printing and server costs. [Clip] An Industry Moving Toward More Structured AI Use One of the clearest changes from 2025 is happening at the organizational level. In 2026, 63% of respondents said their organization is using AI, up from 48% in 2025. Individual use moved in the opposite direction, falling from 46% to 38%. items.title: Report: Oxford Lets OpenAI Train Its AI Models On Historical Texts From the Bodleian Library
items.raw_text: From The Guardian: The University of Oxford has allowed the company behind ChatGPT to train its AI models on historical texts from its Bodleian Library, as tech companies scour academic institutions for fresh data. The Bodleian material digitised by OpenAI has been used to “populate the OpenAI training set”, according to internal documents. Oxford announced a partnership with the company in March 2025, using OpenAI software to digitise texts from the university’s world-famous library, which it said would make the content more widely available for students and researchers. However, the announcement did not state the material would be used for training OpenAI’s models, which are trained to recognise patterns in words – and thus “learn” to write complete sentences and perform other cognitive tasks – by being fed vast amounts of data. [Clip] Meeting minutes at the University of Oxford, obtained via a freedom of information request, record concerns from staff, including members of the Bodleian governance committee, about the reputational risk of partnering with OpenAI and the effect on the university’s environmental commitments of striking a deal involving an energy-intensive technology. items.raw_text: For more than thirty years I have been interested in one deceptively simple question: How do we find things? At first glance, the answer appears obvious. We search. But anyone who has spent a lifetime in libraries knows that searching and finding are not the same thing. Throughout my earlier articles in Public Libraries Online , I explored several aspects of this process. In Finding Answers , I argued that patrons rarely come looking for information; they come looking for answers. In Search vs. Research , I suggested that locating information is only the beginning of inquiry. In Keeping Things Found , I examined what happens after discovery, how knowledge is preserved, organized, and made retrievable for future use. Artificial intelligence is now transforming how people search and, perhaps more importantly, how they find. For the first time in history, millions of people no longer begin by opening a directory, consulting an index, or scanning pages of search results. Instead, they ask a question in ordinary language and receive what appears to be a finished answer. This is more than another improvement in search technology. items.title: How Library Science Principles Power Community AI Literacy
items.raw_text: Public libraries are dealing with budget cuts, book bans, and the usual existential questions about whether anyone needs physical collections when they can google everything. And now AI shows up, and everyone assumes libraries are about to get steamrolled by it too. But watch what’s happening at reference desks across the country. Patrons ask how to determine whether an IRS email is real or a phishing attempt generated by AI. Small business owners are trying to figure out which AI tool won’t steal their marketing copy. Retired community members want to use AI to parse dense municipal documents but do not know where to start. A parent is concerned about their teenager using AI for homework and whether that’s cheating. These aren’t edge cases. This is what reference work looks like now. Much has been written about how libraries can use AI tools internally—chatbots for reference, algorithms for cataloging, and predictive analytics for collection development. But there’s another question we need to answer: How do libraries help communities navigate AI? And here’s what I realized while building AI governance frameworks: these are not computer science problems. They’re library science problems—questions about provenance, access, evaluation, and trust. The exact questions libraries have been answering for over a century, just dressed up in a new syntax. items.title: Tag! You’re It: RFID’s Big Play in Public Libraries
items.raw_text: Radio Frequency Identification (RFID) technology has become one of the most influential innovations shaping the future of library operations. Since its introduction into library settings in the late 1990s, RFID has steadily evolved from an experimental enhancement to a widely adopted tool for improving circulation, inventory management, and patron experience. As libraries continue to modernize and adapt to changing user expectations, understanding RFID, including its capabilities, limitations, and long-term implications, is essential for informed decision-making. This article provides a thorough overview of RFID technology in libraries, synthesizing research, case studies, and industry standards to help public librarians evaluate whether RFID is the right investment for their institutions. Understanding RFID Technology in Libraries RFID tags come in two primary forms: active and passive. Libraries exclusively use passive tags, which do not require an internal power source and are small enough to be concealed within books and media cases. Passive tags contain information that is picked up by a scanner, while active tags emit their own signals. In library settings, RFID tags store essential item information like title, author, call number, and location and can be read without direct line-of-sight. While many libraries offer large print, braille, and other accessible formats, these resources do not address the full range of patron needs. Without intentional efforts to address these needs, some community members may remain excluded from library services. items.title: What I Wrote in the Margins of My Notebook: Reflections from PLA 2026
items.raw_text: I arrived at my first Public Library Association Conference expecting to leave with organized notes, a clear list of takeaways, and practical ideas to share with colleagues. Instead, I left with a notebook full of starred ideas, half-written thoughts, and questions scribbled in the margins. Looking back, those messy notes reveal the sessions that stayed with me long after the conference ended. Conversations about internal communication, programming for older adults, and flexible, community-centered services challenged my assumptions and sparked new ideas for my own work. Sessions including “Becoming One Library: How to Build Better Internal Communications,” “Aging Together: Library Programming for Older Adults,” and “Memory Cafes in Libraries: Creating Meaningful Connections” reframed how I think about serving both staff and patrons. The idea resonated with me because it recognizes a reality every workplace faces: staff absorb information differently, have varying capacities, and don’t need every message delivered in the same format. items.title: Building More Inclusive Libraries for Patrons with Disabilities
items.raw_text: At every conference I attend, I hope to leave with at least one idea I can realistically adapt and implement at my own library. At PLA 2026, I found that inspiration in my very first session: *”Creating Inclusive Collections for Patrons with Disabilities.”* Presenter Courtney Walker, founder of Libraries for All, shared how her experience as a school librarian led her to rethink traditional picture book collections for students with disabilities. She noticed that many students were not engaging with standard picture books, often returning them unread or damaged. In some cases, families stopped checking out books altogether. Seeking a solution, Walker adapted a resource commonly used in classrooms: laminated books enhanced with sensory and interactive elements. By modifying these materials for library use and creating durable books with touch-and-feel components, she found that students with disabilities engaged more actively with stories and enjoyed more positive and equitable reading experiences. Walker now works as a consultant through Libraries for All and collaborated with fellow presenters Janet Cox and Maggie Fox of Plano Public Library (PPL) in Texas to develop a full collection of adapted books. Their team selected popular picture books, organized volunteer workshops to create adapted versions, trained staff to support the collection, and developed cataloging practices for these unique materials. items.title: Information Strategies for Libraries in the Age of AI
items.raw_text: Librarians must actively adapt to an information landscape increasingly shaped by artificial intelligence (AI), search engine optimization (SEO), and algorithm-driven content. During the PLA 2026 session, *”Trust & Verify: Information Accuracy in the Age of SEO, AI, and Algorithms,”* Nathaniel Burnard, Systems Services Manager at Allen County Public Library, offered a practical and timely examination of how these forces influence the way we, and our patrons, discover and evaluate information. As a 2026 PLA scholarship recipient, I had the opportunity to attend Burnard’s insightful presentation in Minneapolis. Burnard began by explaining the differences between misinformation, disinformation, and malinformation (MDM). While these terms are often used interchangeably, they differ based on the intent behind the creation or sharing of information. Misinformation is false or inaccurate information shared without intent to deceive. Disinformation is deliberately false information created to manipulate, mislead, or cause harm. Malinformation contains truthful information that is presented in a misleading, sensationalized, or harmful way. To help identify MDM, Burnard encouraged attendees to ask critical questions such as, “Does this content provoke a strong emotional response?” and “Does it use small pieces of valid information that have been exaggerated or distorted?” He also emphasized the importance of avoiding engagement with misleading content.
